input: This memo looks at whether condition-monitoring sensors should be installed on the pumps at the plant, and it draws on the maintenance records that are available for the last 12 months. There are 214 pumps running at the plant, and over that period the records show a total of 1056 h of unplanned downtime, which is a very significant amount of lost production time. Looking more closely at the breakdown of that downtime, bearing failures account for 48% of the downtime hours, which makes them by far the largest single contributor. A full sensor set for all 214 pumps has been quoted at $460k installed, plus an additional $58k per year on an ongoing basis. In a trial carried out by the vendor on a comparable unit, the sensors were able to cut downtime by 19%, although it should be stressed that this figure is a vendor figure and it was not actually measured at this plant. As a more cautious first step, a pilot installation on 24 pumps would cost $30k over three months. It is also worth noting that spare-part lead times are completely unchanged by the sensors, so that aspect of downtime would not be improved. Taking all of this into account, the memo recommends going ahead with the three-month pilot; the reliability engineering group will own the pilot and will report before the March capital review, and the decision on full installation will be held until those pilot results have been reported.
target: Recommendation: run the three-month pilot on 24 pumps at $30k, and hold the decision on full installation until the pilot results are reported. The reliability engineering group owns the pilot and reports before the March capital review. The plant runs 214 pumps. Maintenance records for 12 months show 1056 h of unplanned downtime, and bearing failures account for 48% of the downtime hours; the bearing share is the part of the downtime that bearing monitoring addresses. A sensor set for all 214 pumps is quoted at $460k installed, plus $58k per year. Against that cost stands one effectiveness figure: in a vendor trial on a comparable unit, the sensors cut downtime by 19%. That percentage is a vendor figure and was not measured at this plant, so it sizes the possible benefit but does not establish it here. The pilot converts that vendor figure into a plant figure, against a full-installation commitment at the quoted installed price plus the quoted annual charge. Spare-part lead times are unchanged by the sensors, and downtime waiting on parts is outside what the pilot can improve. The pilot therefore tests the bearing-failure share of the downtime hours, under this plant's operating conditions, and its report to the March capital review is the evidence on which the full-installation decision rests. What the pilot measures is detection in service: whether the sensors flag the bearing deterioration that precedes failure, on these pumps, in time for a planned intervention to replace an unplanned stop. That is the quantity the full-installation decision turns on, and it is the one quantity the vendor trial, run elsewhere, cannot supply for this plant.
